name: hero-fsync-dir
context:
Durability
The steps people mix up: write vs flush vs fsync vs fsyncing the directory. Each one moves the bytes closer to the disk, and each one costs more than the last.
Postgres and SQLite get this right by default. Most hand-rolled storage finds out after its first power cut, when the file is there but the last second of writes isn't.

name: try-wal
context: Before we call the new store durable, check the boring parts. Every commit goes to the write-ahead log first, and we fsync it before telling the client the data is safe. A flush on its own only gets the bytes as far as the kernel. Compaction writes a fresh file and renames it over the old one, so it also needs fsyncing the directory, or a power cut can quietly undo the rename.

name: try-lru
context: Reads are the other half. The block cache is plain LRU, so one big scan can push out everything hot. MVCC keeps readers from blocking writers, but old row versions pile up until vacuum catches up. And I'd take the memoisation out of the query planner until we know why its plans go stale.
